frase_gancho.texto: A queen hands her king a jaguar helmet before battle.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the palace we move on to the plaza of another great city. Look for a tall stela with a king standing on a bound captive, with curls on either side of his face and a serpent headdress.

guion_corto.texto: This limestone lintel, more than a meter wide, once stood above the doorway of a building in Yaxchilán, a city on the banks of the Usumacinta River, in Chiapas. It shows a scene that took place, according to the hieroglyphic text, around the year 724. On the left is King Shield Jaguar; facing him, his wife, Queen Kabal Xook, offers him a jaguar helmet with open jaws and a flexible shield: the weapons for going to war. Notice the details: the queen’s huipil, with its fine weaving, and the jade necklaces. It is an intimate, almost everyday scene, but with a very serious background: the preparation for a battle.

guion_largo.texto:
A couple prepares for war. She holds the helmet; he, a flint weapon. It is an almost domestic moment, frozen in stone about one thousand three hundred years ago. What is extraordinary is that we know their names: he, Itzamnaaj Bahlam, known as Shield Jaguar; she, Lady Kabal Xook.

How do we know? Because the Maya wrote. Around the scene there are glyphs, signs that form a writing system capable of recording spoken language. For a long time it was believed that these signs spoke only of calendars and gods. Beginning in 1960, the archaeologist Tatiana Proskouriakoff studied the inscriptions of Yaxchilán and other cities, and showed something revolutionary: they told the story of real people, with names, dates, weddings, births, and battles. This piece is part of that story.

Shield Jaguar ruled Yaxchilán for decades and raised many buildings. His wife appears on several lintels of this same building. On another, she is shown performing a self-sacrifice: she pulls a cord with thorns through her tongue to offer her own blood to the gods. You have already seen this idea, blood as nourishment, in the [stone palm](mna_s08_palma_sacrificio) in the previous hall. Here the protagonist is a woman, and she does it as part of court rituals.

That tells us something important: among the Maya, noblewomen could have a very visible political and ritual role. They were not decorative figures. Here the queen hands over the helmet, the shield, and the pectoral: without that gesture, the king did not go to war. It is thought that this handing over blessed the campaign.

Yaxchilán lies on a bend of the Usumacinta River, deep in the jungle, and for centuries it could only be reached by boat or by cutting a path through the vegetation. In the late nineteenth century, explorers such as Alfred Maudslay and Teobert Maler documented it, and some lintels from the same building ended up in the British Museum, in London. This one arrived in the Mexican capital in the 1960s, for the inauguration of this museum.

Notice the jaguar as well. For the Maya, the jaguar was the lord of the night, the one who walked through the underworld with the Sun when it set. Putting on its helmet was taking on its strength. You have already seen it in the [stone jaguar in the Mexica Hall](mna_s06_ocelotl_cuauhxicalli) and in the Olmec jaguar child. A symbol that traveled for three thousand years.

Look at the queen’s huipil. It is a garment that is still woven today: in the upstairs halls you will see huipiles worn by present-day Maya women, with designs that recall those of centuries ago. The backstrap loom technique, with which it is made, has a long history.

And one last detail. In the upper corner of the lintel there is a small hieroglyphic inscription that seems to contain the name of the artist. Maya sculptors sometimes signed their works. A sculptor who wanted us to know that he was there. And we do.

Look at the queen’s huipil and necklace
Find the glyphs in the upper corner of the lintel

texto.Period: Late Classic (600-900 AD); dedicated around 725 AD
texto.Dimensions: 0.85 m high x 1.05 m wide x 0.16 m thick
texto.Discovery: 1881, by Edwin Rockstroh, among the ruins of Yaxchilán

texto.pregunta: Myth: Among the Maya, women never held power.
texto.respuesta: Reality: There were queens and noblewomen with a public role. Kabal Xook appears on several monuments at Yaxchilán alongside her husband.
